steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on EmoCLIP, a vision-language method for zero-shot facial expression recognition from video trained with sample-level descriptions. Motivate zero-shot FER, review where ZSL and VLMs stand for emotion recognition, describe our approach (including compound emotions and the schizophrenia downstream task), list contributions, and outline the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- FER, emotion models, and the need for zero-shot methods
- ZSL and vision-language models in emotion recognition
- Our approach: video-text contrastive training with sample-level descriptions
- Contributions
- Paper organisation

steps.text:

  - primary task of affective computing; applications: HCI (cite), education (cite), mental health (cite)
  - Ekman & Friesen (cite): six emotions, later seven with "contempt"; most widely accepted
  - human emotion more complex: up to 27 distinct categories (cite)
  - continuous arousal-valence scale (cite): not objective (cite), not self-explanatory
  - need: adjust to new definitions, unseen emotions, mental states, compound emotions -> zero-shot FER
- ZSL / VLMs
  - ZSL: classify unseen classes via auxiliary information/attributes (cite)
  - emotion ZSL: label semantic embedding prototypes, typically word2vec (cite)
  - hard labels: no semantically rich info, ignore subtle inter-subject differences
  - VLMs (cite) with image-caption pairs: better generalisation + zero-shot
  - CLIP (cite) basis for action recognition (cite), video retrieval and captioning (cite)
  - VLMs in dynamic FER unexplored; video-language contrastive FER works (cite) use class-level prompt learning ~ class supervision, no generalisation to unseen behaviours
- Our approach
  - jointly learn video + text embeddings, contrastive, natural language supervision; Fig. 1
  - encoders initialised from CLIP (cite) since FER datasets too small; temporal module from scratch like action recognition (cite)
  - unlike previous emotion VLM/ZSL works (cite): sample-level descriptions from MAFW (cite), facial expression + context, soft labels
  - inference: class-level descriptions of typical facial expressions per emotion
  - compound emotions: average component embeddings, add to embedding set; no new prompts
  - zero-shot on multiple datasets: invariant to domain shift
  - vs CLIP and FaRL baselines: temporal info + sample-level descriptions help
  - mental health: simple MLP, fully supervised; comparable/better than SOTA on non-verbal schizophrenia symptoms; big gains on affect/expression symptoms and total negative score, similar to human experts

  - EmoCLIP trained on MAFW (cite), evaluated on AFEW (cite), DFEW (cite), FERV39K (cite), MAFW: SOTA ZSL; NESS (cite) schizophrenia estimation with 2-layer MLP, comparable to human experts

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Facial Expression Recognition (FER) is a primary task of affective computing and it has several practical applications, for example in Human-Computer Interaction, education and mental health. Researchers have proposed several models to formalise the spectrum of human emotions. Ekman & Friesen propose six emotions (later seven, when "contempt" was added) as the basis of human emotional expression. This is the most widely accepted model for FER, but human emotional experience is much more complex and varied than the seven basic categories, and recent studies report up to 27 distinct categories of emotion. A continuous arousal-valence scale has been proposed as an alternative to emotion categories, but the scale is not objective and it is not self-explanatory to human readers. So as more fine-grained definitions of emotion get proposed and the categorical models expand, automated systems also need to adjust to new definitions, unseen emotions and mental states or compound emotions. Zero-shot methods in Facial Emotion Recognition (FER) tackle exactly these challenges and give effective solutions for unseen emotions and mental states.

Zero-shot Learning (ZSL) is a machine learning paradigm where a model can recognise and classify objects or concepts that it was never trained on, by using auxiliary information or attributes associated with the unseen classes. In emotion recognition, ZSL has traditionally been done with some label semantic embedding to produce emotion prototypes, typically word2vec. But using hard labels fails to include semantically rich information in the prototypes and it also ignores the subtle differences in expression between subjects. Recent Vision-Language Models (VLM) use image-caption pairs instead of hard-labels and they have shown superior generalisation and zero-shot abilities. CLIP has also been used as the basis for several methods in action recognition or video retrieval and captioning. But using VLMs in dynamic FER is still relatively unexplored. Some recent preliminary works in FER used video-language contrastive training, but they mainly rely on class-level prompt learning. This is similar to class supervision and it is not designed to generalise to unseen behaviours.

- Our approach: joint video + text embeddings, contrastive, natural language supervision (Fig. 1)
  - encoders initialised from CLIP (FER datasets too small); temporal module from scratch like action recognition
  - sample-level descriptions from MAFW as soft labels (unlike previous emotion VLM/ZSL works)
  - inference: class-level descriptions of typical facial expressions
  - compound emotions: average component embeddings, add to set; no extra prompts
  - zero-shot on multiple datasets, invariant to domain shift; better than CLIP and FaRL baselines
  - mental health: simple MLP, fully supervised, comparable/better on non-verbal schizophrenia symptoms; big gains on affect/expression symptoms and total negative score, similar to human experts
- Contributions
  - zero-shot FER from video with sample-level descriptions + dynamic model (CLIP); beats class-level, helps under-represented emotions
  - compound emotions via averaged latents; better than prompt concatenation
  - EmoCLIP: trained on MAFW, evaluated on AFEW, DFEW, FERV39K, MAFW -> SOTA ZSL; NESS schizophrenia estimation with 2-layer MLP, comparable to human experts
- Organisation: II related work, III method, IV results, V conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Facial Expression Recognition (FER) is a primary task of affective computing and it has several practical applications, for example in Human-Computer Interaction, education and mental health. Researchers have proposed several models to formalise the spectrum of human emotions. Ekman & Friesen propose six emotions (later seven, when "contempt" was added) as the basis of human emotional expression. This is the most widely accepted model for FER, but human emotional experience is much more complex and varied than the seven basic categories, and recent studies report up to 27 distinct categories of emotion. A continuous arousal-valence scale has been proposed as an alternative to emotion categories, but the scale is not objective and it is not self-explanatory to human readers. So as more fine-grained definitions of emotion get proposed and the categorical models expand, automated systems also need to adjust to new definitions, unseen emotions and mental states or compound emotions. Zero-shot methods in Facial Emotion Recognition (FER) tackle exactly these challenges and give effective solutions for unseen emotions and mental states.

Zero-shot Learning (ZSL) is a machine learning paradigm where a model can recognise and classify objects or concepts that it was never trained on, by using auxiliary information or attributes associated with the unseen classes. In emotion recognition, ZSL has traditionally been done with some label semantic embedding to produce emotion prototypes, typically word2vec. But using hard labels fails to include semantically rich information in the prototypes and it also ignores the subtle differences in expression between subjects. Recent Vision-Language Models (VLM) use image-caption pairs instead of hard-labels and they have shown superior generalisation and zero-shot abilities. CLIP has also been used as the basis for several methods in action recognition or video retrieval and captioning. But using VLMs in dynamic FER is still relatively unexplored. Some recent preliminary works in FER used video-language contrastive training, but they mainly rely on class-level prompt learning. This is similar to class supervision and it is not designed to generalise to unseen behaviours.

In this work we propose a new approach to zero-shot FER from video inputs, where we jointly learn video and text embeddings using the contrastive learning framework with natural language supervision. The architecture is simple and trains a video encoder and a text encoder at the same time, as shown in Fig. 1. We initialise the text and image encoders with the knowledge of large-scale pre-trained CLIP, because typical dynamic FER datasets do not have enough samples to train from scratch, and we train an additional temporal module from scratch, like previous works in action recognition. Unlike previous VLM or ZSL works in emotion recognition, we use sample-level descriptions during training, i.e. captions of the facial expression and context of the subject, which are available in the MAFW dataset. These work as soft labels and aim to get more semantically rich latent representations of the video samples. Then at inference we use class-level descriptions for each emotion, specifically descriptions of each emotion in relation to the typical facial expressions associated with it. For compound emotions, we propose to manipulate the latent representation of the categories' descriptions in the embedding space instead of creating additional prompts. Since compound emotions are combinations of basic emotions, we average the embeddings of the components and add them to the set of embeddings for each additional compound emotion. We show that the proposed method trained on sample-level descriptions has generalisation capabilities that are invariant to domain shift, since we do zero-shot evaluation on multiple datasets. We also show that the temporal information and the domain-specific knowledge in the sample-level descriptions improve zero-shot FER performance compared to the CLIP and FaRL baselines. Finally, to show how well the representations from the video encoder generalise, we adapt them to the mental health domain. With a simple MLP trained fully supervised, we get results comparable to or better than the previous state-of-the-art on estimating non-verbal symptoms of schizophrenia. There is a significant improvement compared to previous works, especially on symptoms associated with affect and expression of emotions and on the total negative score, which is similar to human experts.

Our main contributions are:

- We introduce a new zero-shot Facial Emotion Recognition (FER) paradigm from video input, which uses sample-level descriptions and a dynamic model. This simple approach leverages CLIP, outperforms class-level descriptions and significantly improves zero-shot classification performance, especially for under-represented emotions.

- We propose a new method to represent compound emotions using the average latent representations of basic emotions instead of concatenating or generating new prompts. It is more intuitive and efficient than prompt engineering and it shows significant improvements across all metrics compared to prompt concatenation.

- Our method, EmoCLIP, is trained on the MAFW dataset and evaluated on popular video FER datasets (AFEW, DFEW, FERV39K, and MAFW), and it achieves state-of-the-art performance on ZSL. We also evaluate the video encoder embeddings of EmoCLIP on the downstream task of schizophrenia symptom estimation with the NESS dataset. With a simple 2-layer MLP we get results comparable to or better than previous state-of-the-art methods and comparable to human experts.

The rest of the paper is organised like this. Section II discusses related literature, Section III introduces our methodology, Section IV reports results on zero-shot FER for simple and compound emotions and on the downstream task of schizophrenia symptom estimation, and Section V concludes the paper.

In this work, we propose a novel approach to zero-shot FER from video inputs that jointly learns video and text embeddings, using the contrastive learning framework with natural language supervision. The network architecture is simple and trains a video and a text encoder concurrently, as shown in Fig. 1. The text and image encoders are initialised with the knowledge of large-scale pre-trained CLIP [11], as typical dynamic FER datasets do not have enough samples to train from scratch, and we train an additional temporal module from scratch, similar to previous works in action recognition [22,15]. In contrast to previous VLM or ZSL works in emotion recognition [10,9,20,21], we use sample-level descriptions during training, i.e. captions of the subject's facial expression and context, which are available in the MAFW [23] dataset. These act as soft labels and aim to achieve more semantically rich latent representations of the video samples. During inference, we then use class-level descriptions for each emotion; specifically, we generate descriptions of each emotion in relation to the typical facial expressions associated with it. For compound emotions, we propose manipulating the latent representation of the categories' descriptions in the embedding space rather than creating additional prompts. As compound emotions are combinations of basic emotions, we average the embeddings of the components and add them to the set of embeddings for each additional compound emotion. We show that the proposed methodology trained on sample-level descriptions has generalisation capabilities invariant to domain shift, as we perform zero-shot evaluation on multiple datasets. We also show that, compared to the CLIP and FaRL baselines, the temporal information and the domain-specific knowledge of the sample-level descriptions improve the zero-shot performance of FER. Finally, to show the generalisation ability of the representations obtained from the video encoder, we adapt them to the domain of mental health. Using a simple MLP trained in a fully supervised manner, we achieve results comparable to or better than the previous state-of-the-art on estimating non-verbal symptoms of schizophrenia. We see a significant improvement compared to previous works, particularly on symptoms associated with affect and expression of emotions as well as on the total negative score, which is similar to human experts.

Our main contributions can be summarised as follows:

- Our paper introduces a novel zero-shot Facial Emotion Recognition (FER) paradigm from video input, employing sample-level descriptions and a dynamic model. This straightforward approach, which leverages CLIP [11], outperforms class-level descriptions and significantly improves zero-shot classification performance, particularly for under-represented emotions.

- We propose a novel method for representing compound emotions using the average latent representations of basic emotions instead of concatenating or generating new prompts. This is more intuitive and efficient than prompt engineering and shows significant improvements across all metrics compared to prompt concatenation.

- Our proposed method, EmoCLIP, trained on the MAFW [23] dataset and evaluated on popular video FER datasets (AFEW [24], DFEW [25], FERV39K [26], and MAFW), achieves state-of-the-art performance on ZSL. We also evaluate the video encoder embeddings of EmoCLIP on the downstream task of schizophrenia symptom estimation using the NESS dataset [27], achieving results comparable to or better than previous state-of-the-art methods and comparable to human experts with a simple 2-layer MLP.

The rest of this paper is organised as follows. Section II discusses related literature, Section III introduces our methodology, Section IV reports the results on zero-shot FER for simple and compound emotions and on the downstream task of schizophrenia symptom estimation, and Section V concludes the paper.
